title: Indian IT Firms Hold Margins as AI Revenue Offsets Pricing Pressure
excerpt: TCS kept its operating margin at 24%, HCLTech reached 18.2% EBIT and Infosys vowed to hold about 21%, even as AI revenue passed 10% of sales and clients demanded that AI savings be shared.
body:
• India's largest IT services firms held operating margins through the September quarter even as clients demanded AI-driven price cuts, with TCS at 24%, Infosys targeting about 21% and HCLTech at 18.2% EBIT.
  • AI is now more than 10% of revenue at both TCS and Infosys: TCS annualised AI revenue rose nearly 20% quarter on quarter to $3.1 billion, while Infosys AI revenue grew 29% sequentially to 10.5% of its total.
  • The gains came with a warning: Infosys cut full-year revenue growth guidance to 1-2% from 1.5-3%, saying AI savings are now baked into multi-year client deals.
  • For Indian tech workers in India and the US, the message is concrete: firms are protecting profit through efficiency and AI skills, not broad-based hiring for traditional billable work.

India's IT services majors have closed their September-quarter earnings season with profitability intact, defying the fear that artificial intelligence would compress margins across the roughly $315 billion industry. The pattern was consistent across the largest firms: AI revenue grew fast, total revenue grew slowly, and margins were defended through productivity gains, cost discipline and a willingness to walk away from low-priced work.

Tata Consultancy Services set the tone when it opened the season. Its operating margin was unchanged at 24%, while annualised AI revenue climbed nearly 20% quarter on quarter to $3.1 billion, according to reporting summarised by Finimize. TCS shares rose 3.85% after the results and helped lift the Nifty IT index 3.02% in its best session in six weeks.

Infosys shows both sides of the AI trade

Infosys, reporting late last week, provided the clearest picture of the tension. AI revenue grew 29% sequentially and now accounts for 10.5% of revenue, The Register reported. Total revenue, by contrast, rose just 1.5% year on year. Chief financial officer Jayesh Sanghrajka told investors that volume was softer and price increases were lower than expected amid intense competition, and that clients now expect AI savings to be shared in multi-year contracts.

https://x.com/gaze_observer/status/2115304968487895431

"Growth was below our expectations. Volume was softer, and price increases were lower than anticipated amid high competitive intensity."

— Jayesh Sanghrajka, Chief Financial Officer, Infosys

Infosys said it intends to hold margins at around 21% and pointed to a large deal it walked away from because the return did not meet its expectations. Its internal efficiency programme, Project Maximus, is intended to find further savings. The company won $8.8 billion of deals in the first half of the financial year, 68% of them net new, but still cut full-year revenue growth guidance to 1-2% from the 1.5-3% range it gave after the first quarter.

HCLTech and the mid-season scoreboard

HCLTech delivered the strongest margin surprise among the large caps. Its EBIT margin came in at 18.2%, which Nomura tied to AI-driven efficiency gains, operating leverage and a richer mix of higher-value services, according to Finimize's summary of the results. Net profit rose 21.2% to 51.32 billion rupees and revenue rose 11.5% to 356.20 billion rupees. Annualised advanced AI revenue climbed to $219 million from $171 million in the prior quarter, and the shares jumped 8.4%.

Across the sector, September-quarter results show AI integration work passing 10% of revenue at the two largest firms, while the Nifty IT index has risen more than 16% in October after falling 27% from the start of the year to early October, according to a Dealroom summary of the season.

Why margins are holding, for now

The mechanism is straightforward. AI shortens software development, testing and migration work. That reduces the hours a firm can bill under the traditional model, but it also reduces the firm's own delivery cost. Where firms reprice work around outcomes, or sell new AI integration programmes, they keep part of the gain. Where clients capture the whole saving at renewal, revenue falls. That is why brokerages describe the current client pattern as funding AI programmes from productivity gains and vendor consolidation rather than from larger technology budgets.

Analysts are not declaring the risk over. BNP Paribas analyst Kumar Rakesh has warned against assuming AI gains will continue to offset the pressures, and Infosys chief executive Salil Parekh acknowledged that pricing pressure is now a board-level discussion with clients planning over three- to five-year horizons.

What to watch next

The next test is whether AI revenue becomes incremental money, spent on top of existing budgets, rather than a conversion of traditional contracts into cheaper AI contracts. Guidance, large-deal conversion and revenue per employee will show that before headline growth does. For investors and for the industry's nearly six million workers, the September quarter proved a narrower point: AI has not yet broken the margin model of India's largest outsourcers, but it is rewriting how that margin is earned.
